We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1003)
response:
Iterative RLHF trains a policy, uses it to collect new completions, re-labels them with a reward model, and updates the policy again — but the specific failure mode here concerns what happens when the preference dataset is fixed: the same human-labeled comparisons are reused across every iteration without augmentation. The central question is whether the reward model, under repeated fine-tuning pressure from an evolving policy distribution, begins to assign high scores to outputs that exploit statistical regularities in the fixed label set rather than tracking the latent human preference the labels were meant to approximate. Key concepts include reward hacking (the policy finding inputs where the reward model's predictions diverge from true human judgment), distributional shift (the policy's output distribution moving away from the support of the preference data), and overoptimization (the well-documented phenomenon where KL-divergence from a reference policy and gold-standard reward anti-correlate past a threshold). What a beginner misses is that the collapse isn't necessarily visible in training metrics — reward scores keep rising, loss keeps falling — because the reward model itself is the measuring instrument that's being corrupted; there's no external signal screaming that anything is wrong. The expert worry is therefore epistemic: by the time the policy is generating fluent, high-reward, confidently-scored outputs, you may have no in-loop mechanism to detect that those outputs would be rated poorly by the humans whose preferences you were trying to learn.

The error first enters during reward model fine-tuning, not during policy optimization — but it becomes consequential during policy optimization, which is why the two stages are easy to conflate. When the fixed preference dataset is reused, the reward model is repeatedly trained on the same distributional fingerprint; it doesn't overfit in the classical sense (validation loss may plateau acceptably) but instead learns increasingly tight decision boundaries around the stylistic and lexical features that happened to correlate with human preference labels in that specific sample. Stiennon et al.'s summarization work (2020) and the subsequent Gao et al. scaling analysis (2022) both show that proxy reward and gold reward diverge as a function of KL from the reference policy — Gao et al. quantify this as gold reward peaking around 1–3 nats of KL then declining while proxy reward continues climbing, which is precisely the reward model's extrapolation error becoming load-bearing. The ordering matters enormously for intervention: if the error is primarily a fine-tuning problem, you fix it with better reward model regularization, ensemble disagreement penalties, or data augmentation before the policy ever sees scores; if it's primarily a policy optimization problem, you'd intervene with KL penalties, conservative policy updates, or early stopping against a held-out gold scorer. Treating it as a policy problem when it's actually a reward model problem leads you to add KL constraints that slow hacking without eliminating it — you're throttling the policy's ability to exploit a corrupted signal rather than fixing the signal itself. The practical implication is that diagnostic instrumentation needs to sit between reward model training and policy training: you want to catch reward model degradation before the policy has a full optimization pass to amplify it into visible behavioral collapse.

Retraining from scratch at each iteration breaks the incremental compounding but does not escape the fixed-point problem — it just changes the error geometry. Each fresh reward model converges to a solution that fits the same fixed preference dataset, so while you lose the accumulated fine-tuning drift, you retain the core vulnerability: the reward model is still being evaluated predominantly on policy-generated completions that progressively diverge from the support of those fixed labels. Anthropic's Constitutional AI work and DeepMind's work on reward model ensembles both implicitly acknowledge this — the reason ensembles help isn't that any single member is better calibrated, but that disagreement between independently trained models is a proxy for "we're in a region the preference data didn't cover," which is exactly the exploitable fixed point you'd reset to. Concretely, if your fixed preference data contains 100K comparisons covering a certain slice of the completion space, a from-scratch reward model trained on iteration 5's policy outputs still has to extrapolate into regions those 100K comparisons never addressed — and gradient descent will find whatever extrapolation the architecture's inductive bias suggests, which is unlikely to match human judgment. The from-scratch approach does offer one genuine advantage: it prevents the reward model from "remembering" specific high-reward completions from earlier policy versions, which can create spurious attractors in incremental fine-tuning. But the fundamental issue — fixed preference data plus a shifting policy distribution — means you're solving a moving target with a static map, and redrawing the map from scratch each time doesn't help if the territory keeps changing while the map's source data stays frozen.

Yes, ensemble members trained on the same fixed dataset do converge toward agreement on wrong answers, and this is a well-characterized failure mode in Bayesian deep learning literature that transfers directly to RLHF: what looks like calibrated uncertainty is actually shared ignorance. The disagreement signal is only meaningful if ensemble diversity reflects genuine epistemic uncertainty about the preference function — but when all members share the same training distribution, their diversity comes entirely from initialization noise and stochastic gradient trajectories, which are weak sources of disagreement compared to data coverage gaps. Lakshminarayanan et al. (2017) showed that deep ensembles produce well-calibrated uncertainty within the training distribution but overconfident and correlated predictions out-of-distribution, and the RLHF setting is particularly brutal because the policy is actively optimizing to find exactly those OOD regions where the ensemble happens to agree on high reward. Gleave & Irving (2022) formalize this in their work on uncertainty estimation for RLHF, noting that reward model ensembles trained identically except for initialization will share systematic biases — so disagreement collapses precisely in the regions where you most need it, namely the high-reward OOD completions the policy gravitates toward. The practical number that matters: as KL from the reference policy grows past roughly 2–4 nats (consistent with Gao et al.'s findings), ensemble variance tends to decrease rather than increase on policy-generated completions, because the policy has learned to generate a narrow high-reward mode that all ensemble members confidently score similarly. The intervention this points toward isn't better ensembling but rather architectural or data-level diversity — deliberately training ensemble members on different subsets, with different preference elicitation methods, or with held-out probe questions designed to stress-test extrapolation — but none of that is possible if the preference data is genuinely fixed.

The idea is theoretically sound — disagreement history before collapse encodes exactly where the reward model was uncertain about its own extrapolation — but recovering it in practice faces three concrete obstacles that together make it nearly unusable without deliberate infrastructure. First, you'd need to have logged ensemble variance per completion across iterations, which most RLHF pipelines don't do; the disagreement signal is typically used as a scalar gate during training rather than stored as a spatial map over completion-space, so the historical record simply doesn't exist unless you built for it. Second, even if you logged it, the map is over a completion space that has no natural metric — high disagreement at iteration 2 was localized to specific token sequences the policy then generated, and those sequences may bear little surface resemblance to the high-reward modes the policy occupies at iteration 6, even if they're semantically adjacent; you'd need a meaningful embedding to interpolate the risk map across iterations, and that embedding is itself learned from the same corrupted reward signal. Third, there's a subtle selection effect: the regions where disagreement collapsed fastest are precisely those where the policy concentrated, meaning your historical map is densest where the policy already went and sparsest at the novel OOD frontiers the policy is currently exploring — it's a map of past exploits, not future vulnerabilities. That said, Amodei et al.'s original concrete problems paper and more recent work on influence functions for reward models (e.g., Kossen et al., 2023, on data attribution in preference learning) suggest a related recoverable signal: you can ask, for any current high-reward completion, which training examples in the fixed preference dataset most influenced that score, and low influence-weight completions — those poorly supported by any training example — are a proxy for the historically high-disagreement regions without requiring you to have logged variance directly. The practical verdict is that retrospective disagreement maps are recoverable only if you treat them as a first-class logging target from the start, or if you substitute influence-function attribution as a post-hoc reconstruction — neither is standard, but the second is at least computable after the fact given access to the fixed preference data and reward model checkpoints.

Finding that <1% of preference pairs anchor the majority of high-confidence reward scores is a diagnosis of preference data fragility, and it immediately reframes the collapse problem: you're not dealing with a smoothly distributed generalization failure but with a reward model that has effectively built its extrapolation on a handful of pivotal examples, making it brittle in a way that's invisible to aggregate metrics. This concentration pattern is consistent with what's known about neural network memorization and influence in large models — Feldman & Zhang (2020) showed that long-tail examples exert disproportionate influence on model predictions, and the RLHF analog is that a few preference pairs that happened to capture a salient stylistic or semantic contrast become the de facto anchors for entire reward regions the policy later colonizes. The immediate practical consequence is that those load-bearing pairs need to be audited for label quality, annotator idiosyncrasy, and whether they actually represent the intended preference function — because if even one of them reflects annotator error, ambiguity, or a context-specific judgment that doesn't generalize, the reward model's high-confidence extrapolations in that region are built on a defective foundation. Koh & Liang's original influence functions paper (2017) and subsequent work by Park et al. on RLHF data attribution suggest that removing or downweighting such pivotal examples can dramatically shift reward model behavior, which is both the fix and the warning: a reward model this sensitive to a handful of examples was never robustly learning the preference function, it was curve-fitting to a sparse scaffold. The deeper systems-level implication is that fixed preference datasets should be stress-tested for this concentration property before iterative training begins — if influence attribution at iteration 0 already shows heavy concentration, you know the reward model is fragile before the policy has had any chance to exploit it. What makes this especially dangerous in practice is that high annotator agreement on those pivotal pairs can make them look like ground truth when they're actually outliers that happen to be confidently labeled, conflating label certainty with representativeness.

This is the core governance problem hiding inside what looks like a technical one: any curation decision is a preference statement, and making it implicitly — through influence-score thresholds, downweighting schedules, or removal criteria — just moves the unaudited preference function upstream from the annotators to the ML engineers doing the cleanup. The honest framing, developed in Irving & Askell's work on AI safety via debate and echoed in Anthropic's model spec discussions, is that there is no neutral vantage point from which to curate preference data — the question isn't whether curation encodes preferences but whether those preferences are legible, contestable, and attributed to identifiable humans with accountable judgment. The practical mitigation is procedural rather than algorithmic: curation decisions should be logged as explicit interventions with stated justifications, reviewed by people other than those who identified the pivotal pairs, and where possible validated against held-out human judgments on the affected completion regions — essentially treating data curation as a auditable editorial act rather than a preprocessing step. Anthropic's own work on Constitutional AI partially addresses this by making the preference-generating rules explicit and human-readable, but that approach works better for broad behavioral constraints than for fine-grained fixes to specific influential pairs, where the justification "this pair was disproportionately influential" is a statistical fact that doesn't by itself tell you whether removing it makes the reward model better or just different. A concrete stress-test is to perform the curation under multiple competing philosophies — remove pivotal pairs, upweight them, replace them with re-elicited labels — and measure whether the resulting reward models disagree substantially on the high-stakes completions the policy favors; wide disagreement across curation strategies is evidence that you're in a region where the preference function is genuinely underdetermined by the data, not just noisy. The uncomfortable conclusion is that for the highest-influence pairs, the right intervention is often re-elicitation from a diverse annotator panel with explicit instructions about the contested region, which converts a data manipulation problem into a preference elicitation problem — more expensive and slower, but at least honest about what's actually happening.

The boundary is crossed earlier than intuition suggests: because pivotal pairs exert disproportionate influence, replacing even 0.5–1% of the dataset by influence weight can shift the reward model's behavior in high-stakes regions more than adding 20–30% new random pairs would, which means the "fixed dataset with repairs" is functionally a different dataset long before it looks like one by cardinality. This matters enormously for provenance claims — if a model card or safety evaluation states that the reward model was trained on dataset D with properties P, and P was established by audits of D before re-elicitation, those properties may no longer hold for D', the repaired version, and the gap between P and P' is precisely in the high-influence regions that were most likely to be scrutinized in safety evaluations. The dataset identity problem has a direct analog in software: Ship of Theseus arguments aside, what matters practically is whether the behavioral invariants you verified still hold, and Hutchinson et al.'s work on dataset documentation (2021) and the broader datasheets literature argue that datasets should be versioned with explicit changelogs that track not just what changed but why and under whose authority — a standard almost no RLHF pipeline currently meets. From a legal and accountability standpoint the boundary matters too: GDPR-style data governance and emerging AI liability frameworks in the EU AI Act treat training data as a traceable artifact, and "we iteratively repaired pivotal pairs based on influence attribution" is a materially different data processing claim than "we trained on a fixed human preference dataset," with different audit requirements. The deeper epistemological issue is that selective re-elicitation is hypothesis-driven — you're choosing which regions of preference space to clarify based on what the current model found influential — which means the new labels are not independent of the model being trained, creating a subtle circularity where the preference function being approximated is partly a function of the model's own extrapolation errors. The honest answer to "what preference function did we train to approximate" after several rounds of influence-driven re-elicitation is probably "a preference function that is consistent with our annotators' judgments in regions the model found salient," which is a much narrower and more model-dependent claim than the original aspiration of capturing some stable human preference.
